Mission Architect: Beyond Earth

We developed Mission Architect: Beyond Earth, an interactive, browser-based space mission design game that makes complex aerospace engineering concepts engaging and accessible. Through our game, players step into the role of mission designers, selecting spacecraft components, scientific instruments, orbits, and launch vehicles to achieve scientific objectives while balancing constraints such as mass, power, communication, data, and budget.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by transforming the complexities of space mission planning into a hands-on gaming experience. We enable players to explore how different engineering decisions affect mission feasibility, scientific success, and overall mission outcomes.

By combining a retro-inspired space game interface with real mission design concepts, we aim to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application. Our project encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, and resource management while making space exploration more interactive and enjoyable. Through Mission Architect, we hope to inspire students and aspiring engineers to explore the fascinating world of space science and mission engineering.
details:
Project Details – Mission Architect: Beyond Earth

What does our project do, and how does it work?

We developed Mission Architect: Beyond Earth, a browser-based, 2D retro-style space mission design game that allows players to experience the process of planning and designing a space mission. Our project directly addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by making the interconnected decisions involved in complete space mission design interactive and understandable.

Players take on the role of mission architects at a fictional space agency. They begin by selecting a mission and understanding its scientific objective, requirements, and budget. They then design their spacecraft by selecting components, scientific instruments, subsystems, an appropriate orbit, and a launch vehicle.

Throughout the design process, players must balance important engineering constraints such as spacecraft mass, power requirements, communication capability, data handling, mission lifetime, and financial cost. Once the design is submitted, our evaluation system assesses its suitability, checks critical feasibility constraints, calculates a mission score, and determines the mission outcome and financial result. Players can understand the consequences of their decisions and improve their designs through experimentation.

What benefits does our project provide?

Our project makes space mission engineering more accessible by converting complex aerospace concepts into an engaging learning experience. Instead of only learning about spacecraft design through theoretical explanations, players can actively experiment with different configurations and observe their effects.

The game encourages:

  • Critical thinking: Players analyze mission objectives and make informed engineering decisions.
  • Problem-solving: Players identify and overcome design limitations.
  • Resource management: Players balance mass, power, budget, communications, and other constraints.
  • Scientific understanding: Players learn how spacecraft subsystems and mission parameters interact.
  • Experiential learning: Players understand concepts through experimentation, feedback, and iteration.

What is the intended impact of our project?

Our intended impact is to make space science and mission engineering more approachable, particularly for students and aspiring engineers. We aim to bridge the gap between theoretical aerospace knowledge and practical mission planning by providing an interactive environment where users can learn through their own decisions.

We hope our project inspires curiosity about space exploration, encourages interest in STEM fields, and helps users appreciate the complexity of planning successful space missions. By making mission design educational and enjoyable, we aim to contribute to a more engaging way of learning about the future of space exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use?

We designed our project around a web-based architecture with a 2D game interface and a backend evaluation system.

  • React, TypeScript, and Vite: For developing the browser-based frontend and application interface.
  • Phaser 3: For 2D gameplay, game scenes, and animations.
  • Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui: For styling and creating the interface components.
  • Node.js, Express, and TypeScript: For backend APIs and mission evaluation logic.
  • PostgreSQL and Prisma: For structured data storage and database access.
  • Zustand: For managing frontend game state.
  • TanStack Query: For handling API requests and server data.
  • Zod: For data validation.
  • Pixel-art assets and sprite sheets: For creating the retro-inspired visual experience.
  • Git and GitHub: For version control, repository management, and collaborative development.

Our project is designed to run in a standard web browser on a computer or compatible device, without requiring specialized physical hardware.

How is our project creative and innovative?

We combined the concept of a retro strategy and management game with the real-world complexity of space mission engineering. Rather than presenting mission design as a static educational topic, we transformed it into an interactive experience where every engineering decision has consequences.

A particularly creative aspect of our approach is the interconnected trade-off system. For example, selecting a more advanced scientific instrument may improve mission capability, but it can also increase spacecraft mass, power consumption, data generation, and cost. Players must therefore think beyond individual components and consider the spacecraft as an integrated system.

Our retro-inspired interface, spacecraft-building experience, mission evaluation, and financial outcome mechanics bring together engineering, strategy, and gameplay in a single educational project.

What factors did we consider as a team?

While designing our project, we considered several important factors:

  • Mission objectives: Every spacecraft configuration must be suitable for the scientific goal.
  • Engineering feasibility: The spacecraft must satisfy essential requirements involving mass, power, compatibility, orbit, and launch vehicle capacity.
  • Resource limitations: Players must make trade-offs within a restricted budget and available resources.
  • Scientific instrument suitability: The selected instruments should support the mission’s intended scientific observations.
  • Communication and data management: The spacecraft must be capable of handling and transmitting the data required by the mission.
  • Mission lifetime and reliability: The design must be appropriate for the intended operational duration.
  • Evaluation transparency: Players should receive understandable feedback explaining their score, mission outcome, and design limitations.
  • Accessibility and usability: We chose a browser-based format and a simple 2D retro visual style to make the experience approachable.
  • Development feasibility: As a team working within a limited hackathon timeframe, we prioritized building a cohesive, functional mission-design experience over implementing every optional feature in the challenge.
  • Modularity and future growth: We considered a structure that can support additional missions, spacecraft components, scenarios, and gameplay features in the future.

Through Mission Architect: Beyond Earth, we bring together our interest in space exploration, engineering, game development, and educational technology to create an experience that allows users to explore the challenges of designing a successful space mission.
